questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(6,0.25)$.
Find $P(X=2)$, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Swapped the exponents, evaluating ${}^{6}C_{2}(0.25)^{4}(0.75)^{2}$ so $p$ carries the number of failures.
Left out the factor ${}^{6}C_{2}$, which counts the orders the two successes can fall in.
Used $(1-p)^{n}$ instead of $(1-p)^{n-r}$, so the exponents add to $8$ rather than $6$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(11,0.4)$.
Find $P(X=7)$, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Swapped the exponents, evaluating ${}^{11}C_{7}(0.4)^{4}(0.6)^{7}$.
Left out the factor ${}^{11}C_{7}$, which counts the orders of the seven successes.
Used $(1-p)^{n}$ instead of $(1-p)^{n-r}$, so the exponents do not add to $11$.

questions.question_text:
A seed germinates with probability $0.85$, independently of the other seeds.
A gardener plants $9$ seeds.
Find the probability that exactly $7$ of them germinate, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Left out the factor ${}^{9}C_{7}$, which counts the orders in which the seven germinations can occur.
Found the probability that exactly $8$ seeds germinate instead of $7$.
Took the number of failures as $3$ rather than $2$, so the exponents do not add to $9$.

questions.question_text:
Each of $10$ machine parts is faulty with probability $0.12$, independently.
Find the probability that none of the $10$ parts is faulty, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Found $1-(0.88)^{10}$, which is the probability that at least one part is faulty.
Found the probability that exactly one part is faulty instead of none.
Raised $0.88$ to the power $9$ instead of $10$, using $n-r=9$ when $r=0$ gives $n-r=10$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(14,0.5)$.
Find $P(X=9)$, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Used $14$ failures instead of $5$, evaluating ${}^{14}C_{9}(0.5)^{9}(0.5)^{14}=0.0002386\ldots$.
Calculated $P(X=8)$ instead, evaluating ${}^{14}C_{8}(0.5)^{14}=0.1832885\ldots$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(12,0.5)$.
Find $P(X=6)$, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Calculated $P(X=5)$ instead, evaluating ${}^{12}C_{5}(0.5)^{12}=0.193359375$.
Used $12$ failures instead of $6$, evaluating ${}^{12}C_{6}(0.5)^{6}(0.5)^{12}=0.0035247\ldots$.

questions.question_text:
A basketballer scores each free throw with probability $0.8$, independently.
She takes $5$ free throws.
Find the probability that she scores exactly $3$ of them, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Swapped the exponents, raising $p$ to the number of misses rather than the number of scores.
Left out the factor ${}^{5}C_{3}$, which counts the orders of the three scores.
Found the probability of exactly four scores instead of three.

questions.solution_text:
Success: she scores a free throw.
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(5,0.8)$
$P(X=3)={}^{5}C_{3}(0.8)^{3}(0.2)^{2}$
$=10\times0.512\times0.04$
$=0.2048$

questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}\left(6,\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$.
Find $P(X=2)$ as an exact fraction in lowest terms.

options.why: Swapped the exponents of $p$ and $1-p$, evaluating ${}^{6}C_{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2}$.
Left out the factor ${}^{6}C_{2}$, which counts the orders of the two successes.
Raised $1-p$ to $n$ rather than $n-r$, so the exponents add to $8$ rather than $6$.

questions.question_text: Given that $X\sim B(7,0.25)$, what is $P(X=5)$, correct to four decimal places?

options.why: Swapped the exponents, evaluating ${}^{7}C_{5}(0.25)^{2}(0.75)^{5}=0.3114624\ldots$.
Omits the combinatorial factor and the probability of the two failures, evaluating $(0.25)^{5}=0.0009765625$.
